subject: Critical Thinking
title: Belief Perseverance: Clinging to Debunked Ideas
description: Learn Belief Perseverance: Clinging to Debunked Ideas in one minute.

hook.text: Participants read a study about firefighters. Then they were told the study was fabricated.

buildup.text: Belief perseverance: once a belief forms, it persists even after the evidence that created it is completely discredited.

discovery.text: Ross and colleagues showed that debunked evidence can still leave the original belief standing.

twist.text: First impressions are a form of belief perseverance.

climax.text: The antidote: actively consider 'What if the opposite were true?' This forces the brain to generate alternative.

punchline.text: Beliefs don't die when their evidence dies. They find new reasons to live.

quiz.question: Why do beliefs persist after their supporting evidence is debunked?
options: The mind generates independent explanations that survive the original evidence

details.summary: Belief perseverance is the tendency to maintain beliefs even after the evidence supporting them has been completely discredited. Once a belief takes root, removing its foundations often fails to topple it.
details.whyItMatters: Retractions in media, corrections in science, and updated information in organizations routinely fail to change minds because of this effect.
takeaways: Debunking evidence often fails to change established beliefs
The original belief generates supporting narratives that survive its refutation
Providing an alternative explanation is more effective than simple retraction

faq.question: Why do people maintain beliefs after the evidence has been debunked?
faq.answer: The brain builds causal narratives around initial beliefs. Even when the original evidence is removed, the narratives persist and feel independently convincing.

faq.question: What is the most effective way to correct a false belief?
faq.answer: Provide a compelling alternative explanation that fills the causal gap. Simply saying the old evidence was wrong leaves a void the brain resists accepting.
